Mental Health Care Plan

Patient & GP Details
- Patient: Barbara, DOB: 04/10/1984, Gender: Female, Contact: Not recorded, Address: Fifty Avenue
- Referring GP: Dr. Smith, Practice: Babylon, Practice Address: Not recorded. Provider No.: Not recorded, Contact: Not recorded

Clinical Assessment

Identified Problems/Provisional Diagnoses:
- Principal: Viral gastroenteritis (likely norovirus) — High likelihood (consistent with acute watery diarrhoea, profuse vomiting, subjective fever, household contact/outbreak)
- Secondary: Bacterial gastroenteritis (possible Salmonella/Campylobacter/pathogenic E. coli) — Medium likelihood (ongoing symptoms, fever, failure to respond to ORS; stool testing recommended)
- Tertiary: Foodborne toxin (e.g., preformed toxins such as Staphylococcus aureus/Bacillus cereus) and/or dehydration as a complication — Medium (toxin plausible with prominent vomiting; dehydration risk due to inability to retain fluids)

Clinical Details & History:
- Medications: Vitamin D (regular; dose/route/frequency not documented). Occasional ibuprofen for menstrual cramps (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies/ADRs: Not recorded.
- Past Medical History: No chronic medical problems recorded. Occasional menstrual cramps.

Mental Health History:
- Previous Diagnoses: Not recorded.
- Past Treatments (Therapy, Medications, Hospitalizations): Not recorded.
- Family History: Not recorded (family medical/psychiatric history not documented). Brother and household contacts with similar acute GI symptoms.

Social & Lifestyle Factors:
- Living Situation: Lives with brother and mother.
- Social Support: Family present at home (mother, brother).
- Occupation/Education: Graphics designer; working from home today due to illness.
- Alcohol Use: Occasional alcohol — "a pint from time to time."
- Smoking/Substance Use: Does not smoke. No recreational drug use reported.
- Key Stressors: Acute illness preventing normal work attendance; ongoing vomiting and inability to retain fluids.

Mental Status Examination (MSE):
- Appearance & General Behaviour: Engaged, cooperative during telephone consultation; able to provide personal details and symptom history.
- Mood & Affect: Subjective distress from physical symptoms reported (e.g., feeling "literally roasting"); formal mood/affect not recorded.
- Speech & Thought: Speech coherent and goal-directed; intermittent brief pauses. Thought process logical with appropriate responses to questions.
- Perception: No perceptual disturbance reported.

Cognition:
- Orientation: Oriented to self and personal details (name, DOB, address provided); orientation to time not explicitly documented.
- Attention/Concentration: Able to follow and respond to clinician's questions during call.
- Memory: Short-term events related to illness reported (timeline of 3 days, last vomit ~2 hours prior); formal memory testing not performed.
- Insight & Judgement: Demonstrates understanding of need for assessment and rehydration; agrees to attend clinic for stool sample and hydration check.

Physical Symptoms:
- Sleep: Not recorded.
- Appetite: Not able to retain food or fluids; vomiting everything including water and tea.
- Motivation/Energy: Not recorded.
- Anxiety Symptoms: Not recorded as a formal diagnosis; some distress/anxious tone evident regarding symptoms and hydration.

Risk Assessment:
- Suicidal/Self-Harm/Risk to Others: Not recorded; no suicidal ideation or risk to others disclosed or observed.
- Protective Factors: Living with family (mother and brother), able to pass urine ~1 hour before call (subjective), willingness to attend clinic.
- Overall Current Risk Level (Self): Low for self-harm (no concerns recorded); medical risk: moderate for dehydration/clinical deterioration if unable to retain fluids — requires monitoring.
- Emergency Contact: Not recorded.

Formulation:
- Brief formulation integrating transcript and DDx:
  - Predisposing factors: No chronic medical or psychiatric history recorded.
  - Precipitating factors: Likely infectious exposure from household/school (brother with similar symptoms, reported school outbreak).
  - Perpetuating factors: Ongoing vomiting preventing retention of oral rehydration solution, which may perpetuate dehydration and symptom severity; lack of objective assessment/vitals to confirm hydration status.
  - Protective factors: Family at home, patient able to pass urine recently, engaged with clinician and agreeable to clinic assessment.
  - Conclusion: Presentation most consistent with viral gastroenteritis causing acute distress and risk of dehydration; bacterial infection or toxin-mediated food poisoning are important differentials to rule out. No primary mental health disorder identified in the record; psychological distress is situational and related to acute physical illness.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Viral gastroenteritis (likely norovirus)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Rehydrate and stop vomiting.
  - Return to usual oral intake and normal bowel function.
  - Be able to resume normal work activities.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Confirm likely diagnosis and exclude treatable bacterial causes via stool testing.
  - Assess hydration status and provide appropriate rehydration/medical treatment.
  - Provide safety-netting and urgent escalation pathway if deterioration occurs.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Continue oral rehydration salts (ORS) in very small frequent sips as tolerated.
  - Avoid foods likely to aggravate symptoms (avoid fruit, vegetables, milk; prefer bland foods if tolerated).
  - Attend urgent clinic appointment arranged for stool sample and hydration assessment (appointment to be arranged via support line per clinician).
  - Seek immediate care in Emergency Department if symptoms worsen (inability to pass urine, persistent high fever, severe abdominal pain, blood in stool, fainting/dizziness).
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Arrange urgent in-person clinic appointment for hydration assessment and to collect a stool sample for culture/analysis.
  - Provide oral rehydration and antiemetic therapy if clinically indicated (not documented whether prescribed during call).
  - Consider stool testing results to direct antibiotics if bacterial pathogen identified.
  - Provide clear escalation advice to attend A&E if unable to maintain oral intake or shows signs of dehydration/clinical deterioration.

Secondary Problem: Possible bacterial gastroenteritis (to be excluded)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Obtain diagnostic testing to confirm/exclude bacterial infection.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Rapidly identify bacterial pathogen if present and treat appropriately.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Provide stool sample at clinic as instructed.
  - Continue monitoring symptoms and notify clinician of worsening or blood in stool.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Send stool sample for culture and targeted testing.
  - Review results and initiate antibiotics if bacterial pathogen identified and clinically indicated.
  - Reassess hydration and consider IV fluids if oral rehydration unsuccessful.

Tertiary Problem: Risk of dehydration and/or toxin-mediated food poisoning
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Prevent dehydration and complications.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Monitor for dehydration; provide oral or IV fluids as required.
  - Consider toxin-mediated illness if epidemiology/history suggests shared food exposure.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Take ORS in small frequent sips; monitor urine output and color if possible.
  - Report any dizziness, decreased urine output, or worsening symptoms immediately.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Assess hydration status at clinic; provide IV fluids in clinic/A&E if dehydration evident.
  - Enquire about shared food exposures; manage as toxin-mediated illness if epidemiology supports.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Need for frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution; avoidance of large boluses that provoke vomiting.
  - Dietary advice: bland, simple foods only; avoid milk, fruit, and vegetables while symptomatic.
  - Importance of stool sample for diagnosis and possible need for antibiotics if bacterial cause found.
  - When to go to Emergency Department (worsening condition).
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Inability to keep any fluids down.
  - No urine output or markedly reduced urine output.
  - Persistent or worsening high fever.
  - Severe or focalizing abdominal pain.
  - Blood in stool or vomit, fainting, dizziness, confusion.
- Coping Strategies:
  - Rest at home, maintain small frequent fluid intake, seek family support for monitoring, contact clinician/support line for worsening symptoms.

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Patient agreed to attend clinic and follow advice during call (consent to plan implied by agreement to appointment).
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded.
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded.
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not recorded.
- Review Date: Urgent appointment to be arranged (timeframe not documented). Follow-up to occur after clinic assessment/stool results or sooner if deterioration; specific review date not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus) — High likelihood.
  - Justification: Acute onset watery diarrhoea, profuse vomiting, subjective fever for 3 days with household contact and reported school outbreak; classic presentation.
- Bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, pathogenic E. coli) — Medium likelihood.
  - Justification: Fever, severe diarrhoea and ongoing symptoms not improving with ORS; clinician recommended stool testing to exclude treatable bacterial causes.
- Foodborne toxin (preformed toxins such as Staphylococcus aureus / Bacillus cereus) — Medium likelihood.
  - Justification: Prominent vomiting and possible clustering could reflect a shared contaminated food source; plausible differential pending exposure history.

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vital signs (temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate) — Not recorded.
  - Formal hydration assessment results (e.g., skin turgor, mucous membranes, urine output quantification) — Not recorded.
  - Stool sample results / laboratory data — Not recorded.
  - Explicit documentation of prescriptions (e.g., antiemetic, antibiotics, IV fluids) — Not recorded.
  - Contact numbers for patient and GP practice for follow-up — Not recorded.
● Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None identified. (Transcript supports DDx conclusion of likely viral gastroenteritis; DDx additionally lists bacterial and toxin-mediated differentials consistent with clinician's recommendations.)
● Transcript quality notes:
  - Transcript complete for the consultation; contains occasional brief pauses/unfinished utterances by patient. No major sections unintelligible.
